en: The *Buddha-treatise on Governing the Body*, translated by an unknown person and now appended to the Western Jin Catalogue.
The Buddha said: "One should learn: Are you skilled in speech? As for the practice of the śramaṇa’s Dharma, when sitting alone in a solitary place, one should simply..."
Is one’s intention correct?
Is one consistent in one’s dwelling, one’s reclining, and one’s conduct?
Being centered and upright, one brings clarity to the body.
One who receives the sutras also dwells alone.
To cause even one person among a thousand to be victorious is to be victorious over a thousand armies;
to be able to conquer one's own self is the true victory.
Victory within an army is a victory over those who are themselves victorious; yet such victory is not equal to the victory over all other victories.
To conquer one’s own self is to be forever victorious.
One who lacks strength cannot be victorious, nor can Māra Pāpīyān defeat him. One cannot achieve non-victory; when a bhikṣu is truly victorious, he is invincible.
First, establish the correct teaching for oneself, and afterwards teach others so that they may become like me.
When one practices in accordance with the Dharma oneself first, it is then easy to teach others.
Having cultivated oneself in this way and taught others accordingly, once one has mastered the teaching of body and mind, it is no longer difficult to teach others.
When wishing to teach others, one first teaches oneself; by returning to self-teaching, one gains wisdom through the teaching of the body.
For the sake of oneself and others, let not many people transgress. There is no ultimate self;
because one contemplates that there is no ultimate self, one takes refuge in the body that is beyond fault.
Taking refuge in the body that is beyond fault is not as good as taking refuge in the Truth (*satya*).
Having become wise regarding the Teacher, one becomes wise regarding the refuge; having become wise regarding the Dharma, one becomes wise regarding the precepts.

Among brothers, one no longer worries about oneself and thus becomes wise regarding happiness; one no longer worries about one's own person, for having taken refuge in oneself, one also takes refuge in others.
"One's own person has no limit; one teaches all beings to be liberated from suffering.
He asked: "What constitutes skillful speech?"
The Master said:
"To preach the Sūtra of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment is skillful speech;
to speak in such a way that it does not disturb the minds of others is also skillful speech."
“What is the practice of the Dharma?
It is not to be separated from the two hundred and fifty precepts; this is the practice of the Dharma.
What is meant by ‘one who understands the body’?”
"It means knowing the matters within the differentiated body.
"What constitutes a person among the ranks of an army who can achieve victory?
"It means a person who cannot be overcome by evil."
“What is meant by ‘one person who can master the body’?
It means that when one’s thoughts are evil, one is able to restrain and sever them; this is called mastering the body.
What is meant by ‘the training of body and mind’?”
“It means receiving seven precepts with the body and three precepts with the mind.
“What is it that many people do not violate?
“It means maintaining an impartial mind so that one does not cause others to fall into fetters.”
The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Treatment of the Body
